subtitle: Retrieve fast, then re-rank carefully: how two-stage search works, why cross-encoders are accurate but costly, and what it does and doesn't tell you about Google.
outcomes: Tell a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder apart
Explain why cross-encoders only re-rank a short list
intro: Scoring every document with the most accurate model would be far too slow. So many search systems work in two stages: a fast first pass finds candidates, then a heavier model re-scores just those.
This course uses Nogueira and Cho's paper Passage Re-ranking with BERT, the Sentence Transformers documentation, and Google's own descriptions of its ranking systems.
A research paper shows what a method is. It isn't evidence of what Google runs, and lessons for your site are labelled practitioner judgement.

lessons.title: Two stages
objectives: Describe the first and second stages
Explain why the second stage is applied to fewer documents
Explain why missing candidates can't be rescued

beats.caption: In the first stage, a large number (for example, a thousand) of possibly relevant documents are retrieved.
They're retrieved from a corpus by a standard mechanism, such as BM25.
Then each of these documents is scored and re-ranked by a more computationally-intensive method.
Nogueira and Cho used BERT for that second stage: query-based passage re-ranking.
Practitioner inference: a document stage one never retrieves can't be promoted by stage two.

blocks.text: Nogueira and Cho describe a common pattern. First, a large number, for example a thousand, of possibly relevant documents are retrieved from a corpus by a standard mechanism, such as BM25.
Then each of these documents is scored and re-ranked by a more computationally-intensive method. Their paper describes a simple re-implementation of BERT for query-based passage re-ranking.

items.name: Stage 1: retrieve
items.text: A standard mechanism such as BM25 pulls possibly relevant documents from the whole corpus.

items.name: Stage 2: re-rank
items.text: A more computationally-intensive method scores and re-ranks only those documents.

blocks.label: Practitioner inference
blocks.text: The re-ranker only sees what stage one retrieved. If the right page isn't in the candidate list, no amount of re-ranking will bring it back.

takeaways.text: Stage one retrieves many possibly relevant documents with a method like BM25.
Stage two re-scores only those with a heavier method.
Nogueira and Cho used BERT as the re-ranker.
A page that isn't retrieved can't be re-ranked (practitioner inference).

exercise.title: Find the bottleneck
steps: If you run site search or RAG, pick five queries that return poor results.
Check whether the right page appears anywhere in the candidate list.
Mark each as a retrieval miss or a ranking miss.
Note which stage you'd fix first.
exercise.prompt_template: My search uses [stage 1 method] to fetch [number] candidates and [stage 2 method] to re-rank them. For these failing queries, the right page was [in or not in] the candidates: [list]. Nogueira and Cho describe retrieving candidates with a standard mechanism such as BM25, then re-scoring them with a more computationally-intensive method. Tell me which stage each failure points to and what to try first. Label advice as practitioner judgement.

reflection: How many candidates does your own search pass to its second stage?
Why might a better re-ranker not fix a retrieval miss?
lessons.whats_next: Next, what makes a cross-encoder different from a bi-encoder.

lessons.title: Bi-encoders and cross-encoders
objectives: Describe how a bi-encoder handles two texts
Describe how a cross-encoder handles two texts
Explain how BERT outputs a relevance score

beats.caption: A bi-encoder passes sentences A and B to BERT independently, which results in two embeddings, u and v.
A cross-encoder passes both sentences simultaneously to the Transformer network.
Nogueira and Cho feed the query as sentence A and the passage text as sentence B.
They use the [CLS] vector as input to a single layer neural network, giving the probability of the passage being relevant.
Cross-encoders achieve better performance than bi-encoders, but don't produce a sentence embedding.

blocks.text: The Sentence Transformers documentation describes a bi-encoder this way: we pass to a BERT independently the sentences A and B, which result in the sentence embeddings u and v. The two vectors are then compared.

A cross-encoder passes both sentences simultaneously to the Transformer network. Nogueira and Cho do this for search: they feed the query as sentence A and the passage text as sentence B, and truncate the query to at most 64 tokens.
They use the [CLS] vector as input to a single layer neural network, which gives the probability of the passage being relevant.

blocks.label: The trade
blocks.text: Cross-Encoder achieve better performances than Bi-Encoders. But a Cross-Encoder does not produce a sentence embedding.

takeaways.text: A bi-encoder embeds each text separately.
A cross-encoder reads the query and passage together.
BERT's [CLS] output gives a probability that the passage is relevant.
Cross-encoders score better but produce no reusable embedding.

exercise.title: Spot the architecture
steps: List the models in your search or RAG stack.
For each, note whether it outputs an embedding or a score for a pair.
Mark embedding models as bi-encoders and pair scorers as cross-encoders.
Note which stage each one runs in.
exercise.prompt_template: My search stack uses these models: [list with what each outputs]. The Sentence Transformers docs say a bi-encoder passes sentences to BERT independently and produces embeddings, while a cross-encoder passes both sentences simultaneously and doesn't produce an embedding. Classify each of my models and tell me which stage it fits. Label anything you infer as practitioner judgement.

reflection: Why might reading the query and passage together give a better score?
What can you do with an embedding that you can't do with a pair score?
lessons.whats_next: Next, why cross-encoders only re-rank a short list.

lessons.title: Why only a short list
objectives: Explain why cross-encoders can't be precomputed
Describe the combined bi-encoder and cross-encoder pattern
State the BERT re-ranker's reported result

scene.title: Pay for accuracy where it counts

beats.caption: Because they don't produce embeddings, cross-encoders are not practical for many applications.
The docs' example: clustering 10,000 sentences would need about 50 million combinations, about 65 hours.
The fix: first use an efficient bi-encoder to retrieve e.g. the top-100 most similar sentences.
Then use a cross-encoder to re-rank these 100 hits.
Nogueira and Cho's BERT re-ranker topped MS MARCO, beating the previous best by 27% (relative) in MRR@10.

blocks.text: A cross-encoder needs the query to score each document, so there's nothing to compute ahead of time. The Sentence Transformers docs say that for many applications cross-encoders are not practical, as they do not produce embeddings.
The docs' example: clustering 10,000 sentences with a cross-encoder would require computing similarity scores for about 50 million sentence combinations, which takes about 65 hours.

items.text: First, you use an efficient bi-encoder to retrieve e.g. the top-100 most similar sentences for a query.
Then you use a cross-encoder to re-rank these 100 hits.

blocks.label: Research finding
blocks.text: Nogueira and Cho's system was the top entry in the leaderboard of the MS MARCO passage retrieval task, outperforming the previous state of the art by 27% (relative) in MRR@10.

takeaways.text: Cross-encoders can't be precomputed, so they're costly at scale.
A bi-encoder retrieves a short list; a cross-encoder re-ranks it.
The BERT re-ranker beat the previous best by 27% relative in MRR@10.

exercise.title: Size your re-ranking
steps: Note how many candidates your search could pass to a re-ranker.
Time how long one pair takes to score, or use a vendor estimate.
Multiply to get the time per query.
Decide the largest list you could afford to re-rank.
exercise.prompt_template: Scoring one query-passage pair takes about [time] on my setup, and I need results in under [time]. The Sentence Transformers docs recommend retrieving e.g. the top 100 with an efficient bi-encoder, then re-ranking those 100 hits with a cross-encoder. Help me work out how many candidates I can afford to re-rank per query, and what I'd lose by re-ranking fewer.

reflection: Where in your own work do you spend effort only on a shortlist?
How would you check whether re-ranking more candidates is worth the time?
lessons.whats_next: Next, what this does and doesn't mean for SEO.

lessons.title: What it means for SEO
objectives: Separate what Google says from what papers show
Explain why being retrieved comes first

beats.caption: Google's ranking systems guide covers only some of its more notable ranking systems.
It says BERT allows Google to understand how combinations of words express different meanings and intent.
Google has also said BERT is never working alone.
A paper describes a method. It doesn't show which pipeline Google runs.
Practitioner judgement: make sure you can be retrieved first, then answer clearly.

blocks.text: Google's guide to its ranking systems says it is a guide to understanding some of its more notable ranking systems, not a full list. It describes BERT as allowing Google to understand how combinations of words express different meanings and intent.
In a separate post, Google said BERT plays a critical role in almost every English query, and that it is never working alone.

blocks.label: Practitioner judgement
blocks.text: None of this confirms a BM25-then-BERT re-ranking pipeline in Google Search. Treat claims that it does as unconfirmed.
Use this checklist when advice leans on re-ranking research.

items.text: In two-stage systems, the re-ranker only scores documents the first stage retrieved. This is practitioner inference for any engine.
First-stage methods such as BM25 match terms, so the words people search still matter.
Re-rankers read the query and passage together, so a passage that plainly answers the query is easier to score as relevant (practitioner inference).
Ask for the source. A paper shows a method, not Google's systems.

takeaways.text: Google's guide covers only some notable ranking systems.
Google says BERT helps it understand how word combinations express meaning and intent.
Re-ranking papers don't confirm Google's pipeline.
Being retrieved comes before being re-ranked (practitioner inference).

exercise.title: Audit a claim
steps: Find an SEO article or deck that says Google re-ranks with a specific model.
Mark each source as Google documentation, a research paper, or opinion.
Rewrite the claim so it only says what the sources support.
exercise.prompt_template: Here's a claim about how Google re-ranks results, with its sources: [paste]. Google's ranking systems guide says it covers some of its more notable systems and that BERT helps it understand how combinations of words express meaning and intent; Nogueira and Cho's paper describes a BERT re-ranking method, not Google's pipeline. Rewrite the claim so it says only what the sources support, and list what stays unconfirmed.

reflection: Which SEO advice you've heard rests on a research paper rather than Google's documentation?
How would you explain the two-stage idea to a client without over-claiming?
lessons.whats_next: That's the last lesson. Next, the conclusion pulls the four lessons together.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Two-stage search retrieves many candidates with a fast method like BM25, then re-scores only those with a heavier model. A bi-encoder embeds texts separately; a cross-encoder reads the query and passage together and scores better, but produces no reusable embedding, so it's too costly to run on everything. The usual pattern is to retrieve a short list, then cross-encode it. Nogueira and Cho's BERT re-ranker led MS MARCO, but that's a research result, not Google's pipeline. For SEO, be retrievable first, then answer clearly.

quiz.title: Course quiz
quiz.intro: You've reached the final quiz for Cross-encoder re-ranking. The questions revisit the two stages, cross-encoders and what they mean for SEO.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: Nogueira and Cho describe documents first retrieved 'by a standard mechanism, such as' which method?
options: A. BM25
B. PageRank
C. A knowledge graph
D. Manual review
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: the paper says documents are retrieved from a corpus by a standard mechanism, such as BM25. Wrong: PageRank, knowledge graphs and manual review aren't named as the first stage.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: In Nogueira and Cho's BERT re-ranker, how do the query and passage go into the model?
options: A. Separately, each turned into its own embedding
B. Together: query as A, passage as B
C. Only the passage; the query is ignored
D. Only the query; passages come from a cache
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: they feed the query as sentence A and the passage text as sentence B, so BERT reads them together. Wrong: separate embeddings describe a bi-encoder, and the model needs both texts.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: A paper shows BERT re-ranking beating the previous state of the art. What does that show about Google Search?
options: A. Nothing about what Google runs
B. That Google uses a BERT cross-encoder on all results
C. That Google abandoned BM25 in 2019
D. That every web page is re-ranked twice
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: the paper describes a method and a benchmark result. Google's ranking systems guide covers only some notable systems, and none of the saved sources confirm a BERT cross-encoder re-ranker in Search. The other options all read the paper as proof of Google's pipeline.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: Hypothetical site search: stage 1 returns 50 candidates and a cross-encoder re-ranks only those 50. The best page isn't among the 50. Can the re-ranker move it to the top?
options: A. No: it only re-scores what stage 1 retrieved
B. Yes, if the cross-encoder model is large enough
C. Yes, because re-rankers search the whole index
D. Only if the page has many inbound links
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: the second stage scores and re-ranks the documents the first stage retrieved, so a page outside the 50 is never scored. Wrong: model size doesn't change what it sees, re-rankers don't search the whole index, and links aren't part of this setup.

options: A. Swap in a much larger and slower re-ranker model
B. Improve first-stage recall
C. Re-rank only the top 5 candidates instead
D. Drop queries that use different wording
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: evidence 1 shows the re-ranker works, and evidence 2 plus the two-stage description point to the candidate set as the bottleneck, so improve first-stage recall. Wrong: a larger re-ranker can't score what was never retrieved; re-ranking only 5 shrinks the candidate set further; dropping queries removes real users.
